item.title: Light My Fire in the Shadows: The High-Contrast Universe of BPD
item.description:
Borderline Personality Disorder

Light My Fire in the Shadows: The High-Contrast Universe of BPD

The dual-movement challenge of mutual adaptation.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • While neurodivergence gains acceptance in modern workplaces, BPD remains hard to grasp.
  • Caravaggio and The Doors offer visual and sonic anchors for this high-amplitude reality.
  • The individual works toward stability, while the organization builds trust.

Neurodivergence is becoming a better-accepted word in companies and is increasingly recognized as a legitimate source of workplace difference. Organizations are gradually learning to value distinct ways of perception and thinking, viewing cognitive variation as a potential strength rather than mere deficit. Yet a persistent challenge remains: rarer conditions are harder to relate to, making it difficult for other people to understand both the condition and the experience underneath it.

How can we understand the experience of Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), for example? Diagnostic manuals catalog BPD through clinical criteria: emotional dysregulation, fear of abandonment, identity instability — patterns that emerge from an ongoing interaction between an inborn emotional vulnerability and an invalidating environment (Crowell, Beauchaine, & Linehan, 2009). These are not minor quirks — living with BPD means carrying real, sustained psychological pain, not just an unusual personality style. A list of symptoms conveys little of what it feels like from the inside. An attempt to bridge this empathy gap, partial as it inevitably remains, is to bring together image and sound. The image is a Caravaggio painting; the sound is a song by The Doors.

The Image: Caravaggio's High-Contrast Canvas

Imagine spending every day inside a painting by Caravaggio. In his 1599 masterpiece,

Caravaggio uses tenebrism — an extreme style in which a violent beam of light pierces a pitch-black void. There are no gentle mid-tones, no soft pastels. Ordinary men sit in a dark tavern when a sudden ray of light cuts across the room, exposing raw tension. This visual tension captures something of the internal world of BPD. The darkness echoes chronic emptiness; the blinding spotlight represents acute emotional arousal. For someone with BPD, reality rarely registers in muted grays — an interaction is either cast in obscurity or lit up under a scorching spotlight.

The Sound: The Doors' Volatile Soundscape

Now set that painting to music: The Doors' When the Music's Over. The song doesn't stay in a comfortable groove. It moves through extreme shifts — from a delicate, atmospheric whisper to a thunderous detonation of sound. It mirrors an internal landscape where emotional volume can jump from zero to a hundred in a heartbeat: an agonizing push-pull between an urgent longing to connect and a desperate impulse to shut everything down.

Living in High Contrast: Acute Radar and Interpersonal Friction

Imagine living in a Caravaggio painting, scored by The Doors. It's intense, it's exhausting, and it creates friction with people around you who are settled into everyday routines. In a workplace or a social circle built on predictable rhythms and diplomatic gray areas, someone operating at maximum emotional intensity can appear volatile or disruptive. A person with BPD often has an exceptionally tuned perceptual radar — what researchers have described as an interpersonal hypersensitivity phenotype (Gunderson & Lyons-Ruth, 2008). A single casual remark, a subtle pause in a colleague's voice, or a muted expression— it registers instantly as an early signal, a possible shift in the collective mood; perhaps a sign of things to come.

The Workplace Paradox: A Double Movement Toward Center and Edges

Such situations point to a real workplace challenge: the need for mutual adaptation. Corporate culture tends to be set in its ways and prone to inertia; in the interest of stability, organizations reward predictable, middle-ground behavior. But prioritizing conformity breeds groupthink, leaving companies blind to emerging risks and subtle shifts. Genuine integration requires a double movement, happening at the same time — toward the center, and toward the edges.

  • The Individual's Movement (Toward the Center): The person with BPD often benefits from regulation skills that anchor acute reactions, so hyper-vigilance doesn't tip into burnout or unnecessary conflict.
  • The Organization's Movement (Making Room at the Edges): At the same time, the organization has to move outward — not by treating heightened sensitivity as a resource to extract, but by building enough psychological safety that observations can actually be voiced, heard, and weighed alongside everything else.

Picture a company-wide meeting where leadership announces a reorganization as good news, met with polite nods all around. The person with BPD reads something else in the room — held breaths, worried looks, a question nobody quite asks — and senses the quiet is not agreement. Dismissed as negativity, the unease festers and surfaces months later as resignations. Taken seriously, leadership opens the floor and the real concerns come out early.

Workplaces are not neutral bystanders: the same invalidating pattern Crowell, Beauchaine, and Linehan (2009) describe at home — dismissing emotional signals until they escalate to be noticed — can just as easily repeat itself in a conference room, deepening the very dysregulation it punishes. A workplace that meets heightened sensitivity with curiosity instead of correction can become the needed validating environment. This double movement is essential, but it only occurs as an exchange — what the organization hopes to gain, it must first earn. Trust comes before insight, not the reverse.

BPD is not a broken instrument but is not a gift either. Living with this much intensity is genuinely hard, for the person and for the people around them. Those who walk this path often feel the world's pull sharply, and its faintest dissonance.

This intensity does not have to be corrosive. Evidence-based treatments, such as Dialectical Behavior Therapy (Linehan, 1993), help build the regulation skills to carry the intensity without being overwhelmed by it. None of that dims the light or quiets the music; it simply teaches you to juggle both without being consumed by them.

item.title: Coping With Chronic Illness
item.description:
Chronic Illness

Coping With Chronic Illness

How coping with chronic illness is a form of information processing.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Chronic illness requires flexible coping with stressors.
  • Coping can be seen as effective information processing.
  • Coping is a dynamic process requiring identifying and prioritizing informational signals.
Source: Katie Willard-Virant

The singer/songwriter Ani DiFranco has a song lyric that reads: “Buildings and bridges/Are made to bend in the wind/To withstand the world/That’s what it takes.” I’ve always liked this lyric, as it reminds me that flexibility rather than brute force is essential in coping with challenges. This month’s post will analyze that flexibility as foundational to coping with chronic illness. A new research article titled "Stress-coping-adaptation trilogy in chronic illness management: A new perspective from the granular interaction thinking theory" (Sari & Nguyen, 2026) does a great job of digging into the nuts and bolts of flexible coping. I will present its findings here.

Chronic illness stress

Sari and Nguyen describe stress as “informational entropy.” That is, stress generates signals received by our mind. These signals originate from both inside (e.g., body symptoms, emotions, memories) and outside (e.g., medical advice, family support, social messaging).

Let’s illustrate this with a fictional example: Amelia lives with an autoimmune disorder. She breaks out in a rash on her torso. Some of the many signals hitting her mind include the following:

  • “This itches and burns.”
  • “This looks terrible.”
  • “Am I flaring?”
  • “Will this spread?”
  • “Did my medication cause this?”
  • “What will I do if I have to switch medications?”
  • “I remember when I broke out in a rash six years ago from a medication reaction. That was so painful!”
  • “I am feeling fragile and angry. I hate that I cannot rely on my body.”
  • “Maybe the doctor can’t see me today. I wonder when she can see me.”
  • “I’ve read some stories about rashes that can get pretty bad. I hope that doesn’t happen to me.”
  • “Who’s going to pick the kids up from school if the only time my doctor can see me is in the afternoon?”
  • “I need to finish that work project today. I don’t have time for this!”
  • “My illness puts stress on my spouse, too. I wonder if he can take some of the load with the kids today. I hate to ask.”

Look at all of the thoughts and feelings hitting Amelia at once. These stressors cause an uptick in anxiety and dread. Amelia’s body is likely responding to this onslaught of informational signals with shallow breathing, tightened muscles, and impaired thinking.

Coping

Sari and Nguyen describe coping as the response to the informational signals of stress. That is, coping can be defined as managing the information flow created by stress. Information management consists of identifying and prioritizing (selecting, discarding, and weighing) information signals. Let’s come back to Amelia. Successful coping might look like this:

“A lot is coming at me right now. I’m aware that the stress is impeding my ability to think clearly. I’m going to take some deep breaths, consciously relax my muscles, and bring my nervous system back to a place where my brain can problem-solve effectively.” (Amelia is recognizing that she needs to step back from the onslaught of information and focus on calming down. She’s practiced nervous system regulation as part of her chronic illness treatment, so she knows the processes that work for her and puts them into practice.)

“Okay, I feel better able to think this through. I know that I have a lot of feelings right now. I’m scared and angry and worried. Some bad memories are coming up for me, too, as I’ve dealt with this illness for a long time. Right now, I need to think about what is happening in the moment: this rash. My emotions are important and I can return to them once I have solved the immediate problem, but right now I need to put them on the back burner.” (Amelia acknowledges and accepts her emotions about her illness. She does not dismiss them; rather, she tells herself that she will process them after making a plan for what to do about the rash. She also practices self-compassion as part of her chronic illness treatment, so she is able to put her hands on her heart and say to herself, “I will come back to these feelings and feel them at a time when they can be processed.”)

“As much as I would like to ignore this rash, I know that I need to call my doctor. I don’t know when I will be able to be seen, so I should call now and find that out. My appointment may or may not interfere with tasks I need to accomplish today, but I won’t know that until I call, so I’m going to table these scheduling worries until I have accurate information.” (Amelia realizes it’s not productive to worry about scheduling now. It’s more productive to make the call to the doctor to see what she is dealing with, rather than anticipating problems that haven’t yet arisen.)

“I’m picking up the phone and dialing my doctor’s office. That is the most important action I can take at this time.” (Amelia went through a process of sifting through informational signals until she identified the action step that was crucial: calling her doctor for advice.)

Note that Amelia will continue to utilize coping skills throughout the duration of this flare-up. When her doctor’s office provides her with an appointment time, she will have to navigate managing the appointment with work and family responsibilities. At that time, she will prioritize scheduling issues and make an action plan. When her medical team evaluates her rash and comes up with a treatment plan, she will prioritize understanding and implementing treatment. As the rash is managed, Amelia will prioritize the feelings that couldn’t be fully processed during the acute crisis. She may journal; she may cry; she may talk through her feelings with her spouse or a friend. She’s aware that this step is important in her coping process.

Adaptation

Sari and Nguyen describe adaptation as “the individual’s ability to integrate stressors and responses into sustainable functioning.” Adaptation, then, is the integration of successful coping. As Amelia continues to manage her chronic illness, she can draw upon all of the times she has successfully coped. She can conceptualize herself as a person who copes well with chronic illness stress, which will in turn enhance her ability to cope.

Conclusion

Remember that coping is a learned skill (Booth & Neill, 2017). Therapists are trained to coach you in improving coping skills. Do not hesitate to seek assistance in shoring up your ability to “bend in the wind” and face challenges with resilience.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: When Your Adult Child’s Crises Become Your Life
item.description:
Parenting

When Your Adult Child’s Crises Become Your Life

Love your adult child deeply without living on permanent emotional standby.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • If you let it, your adult child’s repeated crises can quietly become your organizing principle.
  • Repeated rescue may relieve distress in the present but fuel dependence in the future.
  • Stepping back with love can bring both urgency and relief.

Here's a question I sometimes ask parents of struggling adult children. Before I give you that question, I want to add that it usually stops these parents in their tracks. That's because this question triggers them to become much more conscious of the constant grip their anxiety and problematic levels of guilt hold over them when it comes to their adult child. The question is: “When was the last time you made a plan without first wondering whether your adult child might need you?”

For many parents I coach, the answer is unsettling. I hear how they keep their phones close. Some parents have opened up about hesitating to travel or even altering their day-to-day plans. Many parents of struggling adult children share how their mood rises and falls based on whether their adult child is stable, employed, calm, sober, or in yet another crisis. Little by little, their own life becomes organized around preventing the next emergency. I get how there is a huge slippery slope of parents ending up being dragged down by worrying about their adult children.

The Trap of When Caring Is Confused With Constant Readiness

The parents described above do not become consumed with anxiety because they are weak. It happens because they care, but when that caring becomes constant readiness, it can end up trapping them. Sure, any one crisis an adult child faces may deserve compassion and even help. An adult child loses a job, needs a place to stay, or falls apart after a breakup. Of course, a loving parent wants to respond.

The danger is not one act of help. The danger is when helping becomes the default response to discomfort. Repeated rescue often brings immediate relief. The rent gets paid. The anxiety settles. The conflict goes down. Everyone breathes easier for the moment. But over time, the very act that reduces stress today may undermine resilience tomorrow. Confidence grows when people face hard things, solve problems, and discover they can survive frustration. As I have previously written in my articles about the negative impact of overthinking, life comes down to engaging in trial-and-error learning to give adult children the ability to learn and grow from their mistakes.

Rescue Entitlement Dependency Is a Problematic Pattern

When parents repeatedly step in too quickly because they perceive their adult children are in the red (emotionally, financially, or facing a struggle), it puts the parent and the adult child in a difficult position. I describe this pattern as R.E.D.—Rescue Entitlement Dependency. Seeing it laid out with arrows below may help clarify how this pattern progresses.

Rescue → Entitlement → Dependency

In other words, what begins as loving rescue can gradually become expected, and what is expected can slowly reinforce dependence.

That is one reason I wrote my book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!: How to Stop Rescuing, Reduce Conflict, and Help Your Adult Child Move Forward. Every week through parent coaching sessions, I see so many parents who are caught in an agonizing bind: If I keep helping, I may be making things worse. If I stop, I feel like I’m abandoning my child.

A Healthier Option Than Impulsively Feeding the R.E.D Pattern

A healthier path for you as the parent of a struggling adult child is to stay caring without automatically taking over. You can listen without fixing, and what helps is learning to express empathy without rushing in. Once you let your empathy seep in and calm your adult child's emotional reactivity, you can ask, “Would it be helpful for me to listen about what you think your next step is?” This is a much healthier way to engage rather than immediately solving the problem yourself. That shift can feel uncomfortable at first. But it is often the beginning of something parents desperately need: relief, clarity, and the chance to reclaim a life that has been living on standby.

The Takeaway

You can love your adult child deeply without reflexively throwing on your first responder uniform just because your anxiety and other emotions tell you to do so. The more you lead with empathy and gentle prompts for problem-solving, the more you will still stop living your adult child's life for them by making rescues that keep them in the RED (rescue, entitlement, and dependency).

item.title: 5 Simple Steps to Learn Mindfulness That Really Work
item.description:
Mindfulness

5 Simple Steps to Learn Mindfulness That Really Work

If mindfulness has never worked for you, your childhood may be the reason.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Mindfulness is often hardest for people who grew up with their emotions unseen.
  • Noticing and naming your feelings is a skill you can learn at any age, even if no one taught you.
  • As you learn to feel again, you also become able to see and answer your own children's feelings.
Source: StockAdobe/C Malambo/peopleimages.com

Quite some years ago, a colleague dragged me to a mindfulness training for mental health professionals. At that time, mindfulness was not considered a fully valid concept in psychology.

As a psychologist who valued science, I viewed it as nothing other than new age, mystical hippy nonsense. I anticipated a flaky conference, and I was not disappointed. At one point, they had us all stand up and mill about aimlessly while humming for 20 minutes. Then we had to ask and answer some very personal questions with the strangers next to us.

Ugh. Not my cup of tea.

Fast forward to today, where mindfulness and science have met and married. And oh, what a glorious union it is! Mindfulness studies have been pouring from many researchers for over a decade. And the meaning of mindfulness has matured from simply "being in the moment" to a richer, more complex definition.

What Is Mindfulness?

Mindfulness is being aware of what you are doing, experiencing, and feeling in the moment.

Here is a brief list of just a few of the benefits of mindfulness that research has documented in recent years:

  • It helps you sleep better.
  • It reduces your stress levels.
  • It actually changes the structure of your brain, for the better.

Why Mindfulness Is Hard After Childhood Emotional Neglect

I have noticed that certain types of people struggle more with mindfulness than others. In fact, it’s particularly absent and difficult for people who grew up in families that were not tuned in to the present moment or to their emotions (childhood emotional neglect).

Did your parents notice what you were feeling as a child? Did they help you name your emotions, express them, and manage them? Attending to your inner experience, and especially to your own feelings, does not come naturally to most. If your parents didn't teach you how to do this, then you have to teach it to yourself.

This is not about blaming your parents. Most emotionally neglectful parents are loving people who were simply never taught to notice feelings themselves. They could not give you what no one had given them. It's so often no one's fault.

But never fear. Because the good news is, you can! In fact, one of the best things about mindfulness is that it is astoundingly learnable.

article continues after advertisement

Here is a simple exercise that combines both vital aspects of mindfulness: focusing and controlling your mind, and being aware of what you are feeling in the moment. It is taken directly from my book, Running on Empty: Overcome Your Childhood Emotional Neglect. This kind of mindfulness will actually help you recover from childhood emotional neglect.

If you take five minutes to do this exercise three times a day, you are asking your brain to perform a function that is novel. Studies of meditation training have found changes in the brain networks that manage attention and emotion. You are building those networks, and they get stronger each time you use them, even when you are not successful in identifying or naming a feeling.

The Identifying and Naming Exercise

Step 1: Sit in a comfortable chair in a room alone. Close your eyes. Picture a blank screen that takes over your mind, banishing all thoughts. Focus all of your attention on the screen, turning your attention inward.

Step 2: Ask yourself this question: "What am I feeling right now?"

Step 3: Focus in on your internal experience. Be aware of any thoughts that might pop into your head, and erase them quickly. Keep your focus on: "What am I feeling right now?"

Step 4: Try to identify feeling words to express it. You may need more than one word.

Step 5: If you are able to feel something but have difficulty putting a word or words on it, it may help to use a list of feeling words.

If you're having difficulty identifying any feelings, it's okay! Do not put pressure on yourself. Coming up with a word is less important than simply going through the process of trying to focus your attention and feel your feelings.

Imagine that there is a brick wall between you and your emotions. Each time you follow this process, you are putting a chip in that wall. If you keep chipping away, again and again by doing this exercise, eventually you will, bit by bit, break down the wall and gain control of your own mind and access to your emotions.

article continues after advertisement

What I See Now

If I went to a mindfulness training today, I would view it very differently than I did all those years ago. I would see it as a remarkable opportunity to learn more about an amazing, cutting-edge approach to improving mental health in this world.

I would see it as a way to combat emotional neglect in this generation, so that it will not be passed on to the next. I would see it as a tool that can bring calm, and sleep, to anyone willing to invest 10 minutes per day.

Who wouldn't want to take advantage of that?

A version of this post also appears on emotionalneglect.com
